summary: RFC 5444 defines a generalized packet and message format for mobile ad hoc network routing protocols. This document updates it with rules and recommendations for designing new protocols that use the format, so multiple protocols can share it without conflicts.

eli5.summary: If many people use the same shared form, they need rules for how to fill it in so they do not mess up each other's entries.

questions: how to design a protocol using rfc 5444
why must protocols ignore unknown tlvs
subtitle: Mandatory rules and advice for designing protocols that use the MANET packet and message format.

tldr.problem: RFC 5444 defines a generic packet and message format for mobile ad hoc network routing protocols. Some suggested uses of it would block interoperable extensions, waste space or break generic parsers.
tldr.mechanism: This document updates RFC 5444 with MUST-level rules on where information goes, how the multiplexer works and how addresses and TLVs are used, plus recommendations for compact messages.
tldr.outcome: Protocols on the MANET port or protocol number can be extended without breaking older implementations, and can use generic parsers and end-to-end integrity checks.

facts.label: Flags field sizes
facts.value: Packet 4, message 4, Address Block 8, TLV 8 bits

today: RFC 8245 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2017 that updates RFC 5444, and its metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its rules apply to protocols using the MANET IP protocol or UDP port defined in RFC 5498.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 5444 specifies a generalized packet and message format for use by Mobile Ad Hoc Network (MANET) routing protocols. It was designed following experience with RFC 3626, which tried to accommodate diverse protocol extensions but did not fully succeed. RFC 5498 requires this format, and the packet multiplexing process in an appendix to RFC 5444, for protocols that use the MANET IP protocol and UDP port numbers.

Since RFC 5444 appeared in 2009, several RFCs and an ITU-T recommendation have used it. That experience showed how to write specifications that stay compatible with future extensions, produce efficient messages and work with a generic parser. Other proposals would have inhibited interoperable extensions or broken generic parsers. This document prohibits such uses and records the reasoning.

It is not a protocol. Its constraints apply to all protocols running over the MANET IP protocol or UDP port, and are strongly recommended for other uses of RFC 5444. It is on the Standards Track because ignoring the constraints would make extensions impossible, impede efficient messages or rule out generic parsers.
sections.eli5: A shared form works only if everyone follows the same rules. This document writes those rules down so new users do not spoil the form for others.

sections.title: What RFC 5444 Provides
sections.content:
A packet is a Packet Header with Packet TLVs, followed by messages. Each message has a Message Header, Message TLVs, and address information in Address Blocks with Address Block TLVs. A TLV is a Type-Length-Value structure. The Message Header has at most five elements: type, originator, sequence number, hop count and hop limit. These let a router decide whether to process or forward a message without reading its body.

Packets travel a single logical hop, so a router that forwards a message builds a new packet. A packet can mix messages from different protocols, such as NHDP and OLSRv2. Messages can travel more than one hop and carry end-to-end signals.

Extensions work through TLVs: information can be added without making a message unusable to a router that does not know the extension. Addresses are grouped into compact Address Blocks that exploit shared prefixes.

The multiplexer lets several protocols share one IP protocol number or UDP port. It accepts messages from protocols along with the interface and destination, collects them into packets for a single hop, and on reception hands each message to its owning protocol.
sections.eli5: A packet is a mail bag with a label, and the messages inside are separate letters. One person at the post office sorts the letters and gives each to the right owner.

sections.title: How the Multiplexer Must Behave
sections.content:
A protocol can put information in a Packet TLV, in a message type owned by another protocol (only if it is an extension of that protocol), or in a message type it owns. Packet TLVs travel one hop, so they SHOULD be used only for information about the packet as a whole or information useful beyond one protocol.

On transmission, the owning protocol MUST say which interfaces to use and the destination address. Forwarded messages SHOULD be left unchanged apart from hop count and hop limit, which is strongly RECOMMENDED so that end-to-end authentication such as the ICV in RFC 7182 keeps working. The multiplexer SHOULD combine messages for the same interface into a packet without exceeding the MTU. It cannot fragment messages, so protocols must size their messages. It MAY delay messages to build more efficient packets and MUST respect protocol delay limits where practical.

If a protocol asks, the multiplexer MUST include a Packet Sequence Number. This document updates RFC 5444: the number MUST be specific to the interface, kept separately per destination, and either added to all packets or to none for each interface and destination.

On reception, the demultiplexer MUST verify the Packet Header and message layout and send each message to its owning protocol, or discard it if the Message Type is not recognized. It MUST remove any Message TLVs added by a multiplexer extension. The owning protocol MUST verify and process each message and manage hop count and hop limit.
sections.eli5: The sorter may put several letters in one bag and may wait a moment to fill it. When the bag arrives, it hands each letter to its owner exactly as it was written.

sections.title: Rules That Keep Protocols Extensible
sections.content:
RFC 5444 does not require every address to have attributes. This document does: information about an address MUST be carried only in Address Block TLVs. A protocol MUST NOT give meaning to the presence or absence of an address, to the order of addresses in an Address Block, or to how addresses are divided among Address Blocks.

A protocol MUST NOT reject a message because it contains a TLV of an unrecognized type, or an unrecognized Value in a recognized TLV. It MUST ignore them, and MUST NOT remove or change them when forwarding the message unchanged. The demultiplexer follows a similar rule for unrecognized messages: it rejects those messages but MUST still deliver the other messages in the packet.

The RFC explains why with NHDP and OLSRv2. If the mere presence of an address meant neighbor, a later extension such as a blacklist could not be added, because unmodified implementations would treat blacklisted addresses as neighbors. OLSRv2 adds LINK_METRIC TLVs to HELLO messages, and an OLSRv2-unaware NHDP still processes them by ignoring those TLVs.

Other rules include: messages MUST be recognized as seen before by Message Type, Originator Address and Message Sequence Number; addresses SHOULD be in Address Blocks, not TLV values; and a new TLV Full Type should be defined with a rule of only one TLV of that type per packet, message or address value.
sections.eli5: If you see a note in a language you do not know, do not throw the whole letter away. Skip that note and pass it on untouched, so people who can read it still can.

sections.title: Flags and Version Compatibility
sections.content:
The format uses flags fields to say which elements are present: the packet flags field (4 bits, 2 used), the message flags field (4 bits, 4 used), the Address Block flags field (8 bits, 4 used) and the TLV flags field (8 bits, 5 used). All of them are structural, describing what is present or absent, not behavior.

For version number 0, unused bits were previously RESERVED, SHOULD be cleared on transmission and SHOULD be ignored on reception. This document updates that to MUST be cleared and MUST be ignored. A specification that adds new flags MUST NOT use version 0 in the Packet Header, and the new flags MUST describe structure, not other semantics such as message forwarding.

An update incompatible with RFC 5444 SHOULD NOT be made unless there is a pressing reason that cannot be met with a suitable Message TLV or Address Block TLV. Proposals to use reserved flags for forwarding behavior were not accepted, partly because forwarding is protocol specific. For example, RFC 7181 forwards using its MPR mechanism rather than blind flooding.
sections.eli5: Some boxes on the form are marked for later use. Leave them blank and ignore anything written there, so a future version of the form can use them safely.

sections.title: Writing Compact Messages
sections.content:
RFC 5444 has no algorithm for organizing addresses or TLVs, and any approach that leaves the information content unchanged MAY be used. The RFC gives advice for small messages.

A protocol SHOULD compress addresses as much as it can. Addresses in an Address Block share a Head and a Tail and differ in the Mid. An extra saving is possible when the Tail is all zero octets. Splitting addresses into several Address Blocks adds overhead, so more blocks than needed can increase size.

For Address Block TLVs, multivalue TLVs covering all affected addresses are simplest. Alternatives are reordering addresses, spanning addresses that do not need the attribute using a Value that means no information, or using several single-value TLVs. If only one Value is involved, one single-value TLV SHOULD be used.

It is RECOMMENDED that Address Block TLVs with discrete Values define an UNSPECIFIED Value, equal to 255. Also, when a TLV Value is longer than expected the excess octets MUST be ignored, and when it is shorter the missing octets are treated as zero bits. This document RECOMMENDS the same rule for new TLVs. An optimizer MAY be used by the router that creates a message but MUST NOT be used on a message forwarded unchanged.
sections.eli5: If several addresses start the same way, write that part once. It is like writing one street name for all the houses on it.

sections.title: Security and IANA Notes
sections.content:
The document specifies no protocol, so the security considerations of RFC 5444 apply. If messages are left unmodified when forwarded, apart from hop count and hop limit, the security framework in RFC 7182 can be used in full. If not, the Packet TLVs from RFC 7182 still work but its Message TLVs cannot be used as intended. A protocol using RFC 5444 MUST document whether it uses RFC 7182 and how.

For IANA, the Expert Review guidelines in RFC 5444 now also require the Designated Expert to consider the limited TLV and especially Message Type space, and whether a more efficient allocation is possible. Only 224 Message Types are available, so protocols SHOULD be conservative. IANA added this document as a reference for the Message Types, Packet TLV Types, Message TLV Types and Address Block TLV Types registries.
sections.eli5: Keeping every message unchanged on its trip lets the seal on it stay valid. The type numbers are scarce, so asking for a new one needs a good reason.
